title: The Spiders Episode

jokes.text: Warm-up guy tells audience the flashing sign says 'applesauce'
jokes.setup: Warm-up guy points to the flashing sign as if reading it earnestly
jokes.punchline: 'No, no, no, I'm kidding. It says applause.' — A deliberately lame bait-and-switch to loosen up the live audience
jokes.explanation: A thin gag, deliberately cheap — it's a warm-up joke meant to get the studio audience loose, not a real punchline. The self-aware badness of it is mildly charming in context but it's functionally hacky. The show is commenting on the machinery of talk shows.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: No, no, no, I'm kidding. It says 'applause.'

jokes.text: Warm-up guy hypes the audience: 'the better you are, the better Larry is' — implying Larry depends on them
jokes.setup: Standard pump-up speech about being part of the show
jokes.punchline: The implicit joke: a big TV host's success is predicated on whether 200 strangers clap hard enough — subtly deflating Larry's mystique before he appears
jokes.explanation: Works best on rewatch when you know Larry's pathological need for validation. The show is quietly mocking the whole talk-show apparatus from its opening seconds.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: And now, because we've tried it with just the desk... and it really isn't the same... Larry Sanders!

jokes.text: Announcer intro: '...and me, "Hey, Now" Hank Kingsley' — Hank inserts himself into the introduction
jokes.setup: Standard late-night show announcer listing tonight's guests
jokes.punchline: Hank lists himself alongside celebrity guests with his catchphrase, as if he's the real draw — peak Hank ego
jokes.explanation: Perfectly economical Hank Kingsley character comedy. The catchphrase 'Hey Now' and his self-promotion by inserting himself between actual celebrity guests tells you everything about Hank's delusion in six words. Very Tambor.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: My dog ran by and burst into flames... and rolled to put himself out 'cause he read the pamphlets... they pass out to dogs.

jokes.text: Announcer: 'And now, because we've tried it with just the desk and it really isn't the same... Larry Sanders!'
jokes.setup: Standard talk-show 'here's your host!' introduction format
jokes.punchline: The absurd qualifier — 'because we've tried it with just the desk and it really isn't the same' — treats Larry's presence as a minor logistical improvement rather than the main event
jokes.explanation: Sharp, economical, and original. The show is immediately deflating the grandiosity of late-night celebrity culture — Larry is presented not as a god but as a marginal improvement over an empty desk. The dry deadpan delivery is very Larry Sanders. This is exactly the kind of showbiz-insider satire the series perfected.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: because who wants to be in a cast for six weeks? And then, you know, everybody wants to sign it. It's embarrassing.

jokes.text: Larry's monologue: 'My dog ran by and burst into flames... and rolled to put himself out 'cause he read the pamphlets they pass out to dogs.'
jokes.setup: Larry complaining about LA heat — 'It was about 110'
jokes.punchline: Dog bursting into flames is absurd enough; the escalation that the dog read fire-safety pamphlets specifically distributed to dogs pushes it into surreal territory
jokes.explanation: Good stand-up construction. The absurdist escalation — pamphlets distributed to dogs — is the unexpected topper that elevates a generic 'it was so hot' premise. The specificity of 'rolled to put himself out' shows craft. Solid professional stand-up material.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: The next option is a bad haircut.

jokes.text: Vasectomy joke: 'I have never gotten [one] because who wants to be in a cast for six weeks? And then everybody wants to sign it.'
jokes.setup: Announcement that vasectomies lower risk of transmitting sexual diseases
jokes.punchline: Larry's fear is being 'in a cast for six weeks' — a completely wrong medical premise played straight — topped by everyone wanting to sign it, as if it's a broken arm
jokes.explanation: Strong stand-up construction. The premise is deliberately medically absurd (vasectomies don't require casts), but the topper — everyone wanting to sign it — is the real punchline and it lands hard. The image of a genital cast being a social accessory is genuinely funny and specific. One of the better monologue jokes.

dialogue.line: but was still so embarrassed he also bought... an $8,000 toothpaste tube... and $5,000 pack of razor blades.

jokes.text: Larry: 'The next option [to prevent STDs] is a bad haircut.'
jokes.setup: Vasectomies can lower risk of transmitting sexual diseases
jokes.punchline: A bad haircut as a contraceptive method — because it makes you undesirable
jokes.explanation: Very economical — four words for a solid laugh. The logic is sound (abstinence through unattractiveness), the delivery is dry, and it's a good button on the vasectomy bit. Not a showstopper but efficient.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: This is actually the same outfit you wear to drive in L.A.

jokes.text: 150-year-old condom sold at Christie's — buyer also purchased an $8,000 toothpaste tube and $5,000 pack of razor blades so the condom purchase wouldn't stand out
jokes.setup: A 150-year-old condom was auctioned at Christie's for $6,300
jokes.punchline: The buyer was so embarrassed he padded the purchase with absurdly expensive mundane items to disguise it — escalating price tags make the shame funnier
jokes.explanation: The real-world premise (antique condom auction) is inherently funny, but the comedic construction — the buyer's escalating shame purchases — is where the writing earns its keep. The three-item escalation (toothpaste, razors) with ascending specific price tags is solid joke architecture. Good monologue beat.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: He calls it 'the tarantula arm races.'

jokes.text: Larry, putting on hockey gear, says: 'This is actually the same outfit you wear to drive in L.A.'
jokes.setup: Larry is awkwardly putting on hockey protective gear with Steve Duchesne's help
jokes.punchline: Full hockey armor is the appropriate attire for navigating LA traffic — an LA-driver aggression joke disguised as casual observation
jokes.explanation: A competent on-air bit — economical LA traffic observation that works in context. Not groundbreaking but efficiently delivered during a physical comedy segment. The casual, throwaway delivery is characteristic of Larry's on-air persona.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Two minutes ago, you were willing to take a puck to the nuts. Now you're crying over a couple of bugs.

jokes.text: Post-hockey segment, Artie deadpans: 'The audience loved it. Just great. Props.'
jokes.setup: Larry has just done a clumsy hockey segment with Steve Duchesne
jokes.punchline: Artie's single-word summation — 'Props' — delivered flatly, reduces the whole elaborate stunt to a resigned acknowledgment that it was just prop comedy
jokes.explanation: Pure Artie — Rip Torn's character distills complex showbiz politics into a single word. 'Props' is simultaneously praise, dismissal, and industry-insider shorthand. The economy is exceptional. This is exactly the dry, behind-the-scenes voice that makes the show work.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Gigantic fuzzy insects crawling on your body, lions crapping in your lap. It's great television.

jokes.text: Artie describes 'the tarantula arm races': dead fly on head, sit still, spiders race up each arm to reach it
jokes.setup: Artie is pitching a planned TV stunt involving a bug expert
jokes.punchline: The stunt described in full is so specifically ridiculous — a competitive race between spiders using a dead fly as a finish line on a person's head — that the description alone is the joke
jokes.explanation: The invented name 'tarantula arm races' is the kind of specific absurdist detail that elevates a premise. Artie's deadpan explanation — 'dead fly, comme ca, spiders, race, arms, head' — distilled into a telegram-style synopsis is genuinely funny. The repetition of the pitch at Larry's demand compounds the comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: build like this big Santa Fe style Spanish adobe house there. Then you'll be jealous because you can't live there, right?

jokes.text: Artie repeats the spider stunt summary three times at Larry's request, each time shorter: 'Dead fly, comme ca, spiders, race, arms, head.'
jokes.setup: Larry keeps asking Artie to explain the stunt again because he can't process it
jokes.punchline: Each repetition gets more compressed and absurd, culminating in the staccato 'Spiders, race, arms, head' — both Larry's denial and Artie's exasperated efficiency are funny
jokes.explanation: The escalating compression is great structural comedy — Artie reducing the stunt to increasingly telegraphic summaries while Larry keeps stalling. The repetition is the joke AND the character work simultaneously: Larry's anxiety expressed as confusion, Artie's competence expressed as irritated efficiency. Classic Larry Sanders dynamic.

dialogue.speaker: Jancey
dialogue.line: The night is young. Ow!

jokes.text: Artie: 'This is a show biz tradition. Gigantic fuzzy insects crawling on your body, lions crapping in your lap. It's great television.'
jokes.setup: Larry is reluctant to do the spider stunt; Artie is persuading him
jokes.punchline: 'Lions crapping in your lap' — stated with the same gravity as 'gigantic fuzzy insects' as if both are equally dignified showbiz traditions
jokes.explanation: Artie's voice at its best — delivering unhinged content with executive authority. 'Lions crapping in your lap' as a celebrated showbiz tradition, stated without irony, is exactly the kind of line Rip Torn would make legendary. The deadpan elevation of degrading stunts to 'tradition' is smart industry satire.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: They're just the deadliest spider known to man.

jokes.text: Artie chases Larry out while repeating 'Huge laughs. Huge laughs. Huge, rolling-in-the-aisle laughs.'
jokes.setup: Larry tries to exit; Artie is hard-selling him on the stunt
jokes.punchline: Artie's escalating superlatives — each one bigger than the last — expose him as a carnival barker masquerading as a TV producer; 'rolling-in-the-aisle' is the absurd peak
jokes.explanation: The escalating superlatives are a great character beat for Artie — he's a master salesman who never stops pitching even as the door closes. 'Huge, rolling-in-the-aisle laughs' lands as both funny and a perfect Artie signature line. This phrase becomes a callback later.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Watch your step. I mean careerwise.

jokes.text: Artie calls after Larry: 'Get outta here, you big, successful talk show host.'
jokes.setup: Larry exits after agreeing to do the spider stunt
jokes.punchline: The send-off is simultaneously affectionate and slightly mocking — 'big, successful talk show host' said with Artie's gruff warmth, like calling someone 'big man' sarcastically
jokes.explanation: A nice little character grace note — Artie's affection for Larry expressed through backhanded praise. Not a showstopper, but an authentic beat.

dialogue.speaker: Jancey
dialogue.line: having a comedy club in my own home.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Are you saying that 'cause you watered down the drinks?

jokes.text: Unnamed woman's extended mock-paranoid monologue: spiders will crawl on him, lay eggs, build a 'Santa Fe style Spanish adobe house' in his head, he'll be jealous he can't live there, then they'll eat his brain
jokes.setup: The woman is chiding Larry for worrying about the spiders
jokes.punchline: The monologue spirals from plausible fear to full absurdist architecture — spiders building a Santa Fe adobe house inside Larry's head and him being jealous he can't move in — delivered as if these are rational next steps
jokes.explanation: This is the comedic highlight of the first half. The monologue follows an internal logic that escalates perfectly — each step is more absurd but follows from the last with dream-logic inevitability. 'Santa Fe style Spanish adobe house' is a genuine inspired detail; the twist that Larry would be jealous he can't move into his OWN head is structurally sophisticated. 'By the time you figure it out, those spiders'll have eaten your brain out and there'll be nothing left and what's the point?' is a devastating button. This compares favorably to top-shelf absurdist sitcom writing.

dialogue.speaker: Jancey
dialogue.line: Geez, I hope one of those spiders bites you tomorrow night.

jokes.text: Woman: 'You don't relate to the spider thing because you've never had anything big and hairy crawling all over you, have you?' — beat — Man off-camera: 'The night is young. Ow!'
jokes.setup: Woman makes a remark about Larry's spider aversion being linked to inexperience with 'big and hairy' things
jokes.punchline: The off-camera male voice interprets it sexually and brags; the 'Ow!' suggests she immediately hit him for it
jokes.explanation: A solid double-entendre that works because the setup is genuinely ambiguous and the payoff ('Ow!') is quick and physical. The off-camera voice and immediate punishment is an economical staging choice. Not high-concept, but clean execution.

dialogue.speaker: Jancey
dialogue.line: So, can we start a family if I have the baby at the Greek Theater? Huh?

jokes.text: Man: 'Listen, all kidding aside, don't worry about those tarantulas, all right? They're just the deadliest spider known to man.'
jokes.setup: Man is ostensibly reassuring Larry about the tarantula stunt
jokes.punchline: 'They're just the deadliest spider known to man' — delivered as comfort
jokes.explanation: Classic deadpan reassurance-as-threat construction. The 'all kidding aside' setup makes the punchline land harder because it promises sincerity before delivering the opposite. Economical and effective.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: But in the shape of a spider, honey.

jokes.text: Man: 'Oh, you're such a jerk.' Larry: 'Yeah, I'm jerking my way to the bank.'
jokes.setup: Larry's friend calls him a jerk for making a bad reassurance joke
jokes.punchline: Larry riffs on 'jerking' as both behavior and financial success — a quick self-aware pivot
jokes.explanation: A quick, serviceable wordplay riff. Not particularly original but delivered with confidence. The self-deprecating-success combo is a Larry Sanders personality marker.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: Intimacy.

jokes.text: Larry: 'Watch your step.' Beat. '...I mean careerwise.'
jokes.setup: Larry calls out 'Watch your step' as the group leaves the restaurant — literally about a physical step
jokes.punchline: Retroactively reframing it as a career threat/warning, which is simultaneously funnier and reveals Larry's competitive showbiz anxieties
jokes.explanation: A deceptively good little joke. The pivot from literal to metaphorical via the beat is perfectly timed, and the 'careerwise' addition recontextualizes the whole line as an instinctive showbiz threat from someone who can't stop thinking in competitive terms. Very Larry Sanders — his anxieties leak out even in small talk.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Were they Ludes? Soapers? Were they reds?

jokes.text: Larry's partner says: 'Honey, I didn't get a word in edgewise all night. All I said was, "No more coffee."'
jokes.setup: Larry and his male friend were dominating conversation at dinner
jokes.punchline: Her entire contribution to the evening was a beverage refusal — the comedy-club-in-my-own-home complaint is the setup but this specific detail is the punchline
jokes.explanation: A recognizable domestic complaint elevated by the specificity of 'No more coffee' being her only utterance. The show-business men absorbing all social oxygen at dinner is a real observation, delivered with appropriate mild frustration.

dialogue.speaker: Carol
dialogue.line: Ooh, pubic hair on my coconut. That's it. Sexual harassment. Where is my lawyer?

jokes.text: Larry: 'Are you saying that 'cause you watered down the drinks?' — to his wife's complaint about having a 'comedy club in my own home'
jokes.setup: Linda complains about dinner feeling like a comedy club
jokes.punchline: Larry deflects her legitimate complaint by pivoting to accusing her of drink sabotage — revealing his defensiveness and also that he thinks about comedy club economics
jokes.explanation: A quick, sharp deflection that's both a joke and character revelation — Larry can't engage with his wife's complaint without making another joke. Classic avoidance humor.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: They look like big, hairy potatoes with legs in 'em.

jokes.text: Linda: 'Geez, I hope one of those spiders bites you tomorrow night.'
jokes.setup: Larry is discussing doing the spider stunt; Linda is irritated
jokes.punchline: A spouse sincerely wishing spider-bite harm on her husband as a relationship expression — delivered as casual frustration rather than malice
jokes.explanation: A nice dark comedy domestic beat — the naturalistic venom of the wish (combined with 'Geez') makes it funnier than an outright angry statement. The casualness of the dark sentiment is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: They're roller coasters. Call it what you like.

jokes.text: Larry: 'Now you're hurting me. Why are you hurting me? You know that I'm afraid of spiders.'
jokes.setup: Linda wishes a spider would bite him
jokes.punchline: Larry's reaction to an idle remark as genuine emotional injury — treating his spider phobia as a protected vulnerability that Linda is weaponizing
jokes.explanation: Pure Larry Sanders character comedy — his fragile sensitivity rendered in a domestic setting. The escalation from spider fear to emotional injury is funny because he's treating a mild comment like a personal betrayal. Tambor/Shandling dynamic prototype.

dialogue.speaker: Writer
dialogue.line: I think he's trying out a new Lebanese thing.

jokes.text: Linda: 'You guys will do anything for a laugh.' Larry: 'That is not true.' Linda: 'Yes, it is. Then why are you doing it?' Larry: 'Because it'll be funny.'
jokes.setup: Linda accuses Larry of doing dangerous stunts purely for laughs
jokes.punchline: Larry denies it, then immediately confirms it — 'Because it'll be funny' — completing the circular logic in three lines
jokes.explanation: Beautifully structured three-line exchange. The denial followed immediately by the confession ('Because it'll be funny') is a perfect comedic circle — Larry disproves his own assertion in one breath. This is both a great joke and a sharp encapsulation of show-business pathology: performers will endure real discomfort to generate a staged reaction. Highly efficient, character-specific, and structurally clean.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: You know, talking to you is like talking to you.

jokes.text: Linda: 'You're willing to confront your fears if it's in front of 20 million people and for a laugh? So, can we start a family if I have the baby at the Greek Theater?'
jokes.setup: Larry says he should confront his spider fear 'for himself' — but it's clearly for the show
jokes.punchline: Linda extrapolates: if fear-confrontation only counts in public for laughs, then childbirth should be a live performance event at the Greek Theater
jokes.explanation: A genuinely sharp piece of writing. The Greek Theater punchline extends Larry's performative logic to its absurd conclusion — if everything personal must become a public spectacle, then childbirth should be ticketed. It's funny AND a precise critique of Larry's character: his inability to experience anything privately. One of the better lines in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Yes, it is. The fastest light in the West. Fire 'em up, partner.

jokes.text: Larry shows Linda a sock — she says it's just a sock — Larry: 'But in the shape of a spider, honey.'
jokes.setup: Larry is apparently trying to scare or tease Linda with something
jokes.punchline: It's a sock. Shaped vaguely like a spider. Larry treats it as a legitimate spider-shaped object worthy of annotation.
jokes.explanation: A light visual gag — the comedy is in the visual of a man defending his sock as meaningfully spider-shaped. The 'honey' tag is a nice Larry touch. Slight but functional.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Stunts are Larry's territory. Hank Kingsley shalt not trespass.

jokes.text: Larry asks his assistant if she's afraid of anything. She says: 'Intimacy.' Long beat. 'Anything more you wanna tell me?'
jokes.setup: Larry, preoccupied with his spider fear, asks his assistant what she's afraid of — expecting a relatable answer
jokes.punchline: 'Intimacy' — one word, delivered flatly, which both lands as a joke and immediately shuts down any follow-up; Larry's non-reaction is the beat
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's funniest single-word jokes. 'Intimacy' as a deadpan answer to 'what are you afraid of?' is funny on its own, but the follow-up beat — Larry not knowing what to do with it, asking 'Anything more you wanna tell me?' — is perfect. Maximum funny per word. The joke works because it's both an unexpected answer AND a complete character portrait in one syllable. Near-perfect economy.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Not that I've made a stink about it, because I am not... a squeaky wheel, you know that.

jokes.text: Larry's escalating drug inquiry: 'Now how do you overcome it? / Tranquilizers. / What were they? Xanaxes? Valiums? Halcyons? / ...Were they Ludes? Soapers? / Were they reds?'
jokes.setup: Beverly reveals she overcomes flying fear with tranquilizers; Larry wants details
jokes.punchline: Larry's inquiry escalates from reasonable (Xanax, Valium) to vintage recreational drugs (Quaaludes/Ludes, Soapers) to full street-drug nostalgia (reds), each refusal from Beverly met with a more obscure and increasingly illegal pharmaceutical
jokes.explanation: A structurally excellent escalating bit. The progression from clinical pharmaceuticals to increasingly retro/illegal drugs is perfectly calibrated — 'Ludes? Soapers?' is the escalation peak (both deeply 1970s Hollywood), and Beverly's increasing urgency ('Now you got one minute... now you got one') layered over Larry's drug archaeology is a beautifully constructed comedic counterpoint. Deeply Larry: his anxiety instantly transforms into pharmaceutical procurement. One of the episode's most sharply written exchanges.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: The hat?

jokes.text: Carol Burnett Tarzan sketch — Larry flubs his line: 'Shit. Me Tarzan, you Jane.' Carol: 'That's Ms. Jane to you.'
jokes.setup: Larry is rehearsing a Tarzan/Jane sketch with Carol Burnett and forgets his line
jokes.punchline: Carol instantly improvises a feminist corrective ('Ms. Jane') — both funny as a punchline and a character grace note showing her quick wit
jokes.explanation: A lovely quick joke. Carol Burnett playing herself and instantly riffing a feminist corrective to a classic sexist trope is both funny and perfectly in-character for her persona. The swear establishing it's a flub, then the snap comeback — clean construction. Elevated by who's delivering it.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Between you and me, I think I saw your balls at one point.

jokes.text: Larry during Tarzan sketch: 'Mmm, would you like some coco— Ooh, pubic hair on my coconut.'
jokes.setup: Larry is trying to deliver a line about coconut juice in the sketch
jokes.punchline: He discovers what appears to be pubic hair on the prop coconut mid-line — the specificity of 'pubic' mid-character-voice is the shock laugh
jokes.explanation: A good prop-comedy gag — the contrast between the gentle character-voice delivery and the jarring discovery of 'pubic hair' is the shock. Works in context, probably funnier visually than on paper.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Did you really see my balls?

jokes.text: Carol immediately launches into a sexual harassment lawsuit bit: 'Nairobi and Meyers. On behalf of my client we are filing charges of sexual misconduct... You shall not come within 500 yards of my client.'
jokes.setup: Larry discovers pubic hair on a prop coconut during rehearsal
jokes.punchline: Carol immediately pivots to a fully formed legal proceedings bit, naming a law firm and issuing a restraining order — treating a prop mishap as a federal harassment case
jokes.explanation: Carol Burnett's improv instinct elevated into a bit — the instant escalation to a formal legal framework ('Nairobi and Meyers') for a prop comedy mishap is funny because of the disproportionate formality. The 500-yard restraining order from a coconut is absurd and well-committed.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: That's my cup from the hockey segment.

jokes.text: Larry mid-sketch, genuinely confused: 'I don't know where we are. Are we doing this sketch before the spiders or after them?'
jokes.setup: Larry is already so anxious about the spider stunt that he can't maintain focus during a sketch rehearsal with Carol Burnett
jokes.punchline: He breaks character to ask a logistical question about the spider scheduling — revealing his anxiety is consuming him even in front of a legend
jokes.explanation: Good character comedy — Larry's inability to compartmentalize his spider anxiety even during rehearsal with Carol Burnett reveals the scale of his preoccupation. The specific question ('before the spiders or after them?') is both funny and pathetically relatable.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: My God... you're a good man.

jokes.text: Larry describes the tarantulas backstage: 'They look like big, hairy potatoes with legs in 'em. I'm gonna have dreams.'
jokes.setup: Larry has just seen the spiders backstage and is reporting back to Artie in a panic
jokes.punchline: 'Big, hairy potatoes with legs in 'em' is a genuinely original simile; 'I'm gonna have dreams' as a trailing horror-anticipation is the button
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. 'Big, hairy potatoes with legs in 'em' is a memorably specific and original description — not the expected 'disgusting' or 'huge,' but a domestic food item transformed into a nightmare. The 'in 'em' grammatical stumble makes it feel authentic rather than polished. 'I'm gonna have dreams' as a flat prediction of future trauma is a perfect quiet topper. Highly quotable, genuinely original phrasework.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Hank, please.

jokes.text: Larry corrects Artie: 'They're roller coasters.' Artie: 'Call it what you like. I'd never get on the damn thing.'
jokes.setup: Artie has said 'rolly-coasters'
jokes.punchline: 'Call it what you like' — Artie refuses to be corrected on his own mispronunciation, dismissing the correction as a matter of personal preference
jokes.explanation: Rip Torn's Artie refusing to accept a correction of his own malapropism — 'call it what you like' — is a perfect character beat. The dismissal of factual correction as a matter of preference is deeply funny and character-specific. Artie's supreme self-confidence in his own wrongness is quintessential.

dialogue.line: Could you take your top off? I'm begging you. Could you?

jokes.text: Writers mock Larry's rehearsal: 'He doesn't know what he's doing. His timing's a mess. He was all over the place.' Writer: 'That voice, did you hear that Tarzan voice? What was that?' Other writer: 'I think he's trying out a new Lebanese thing.'
jokes.setup: Writers are watching Larry's terrible Tarzan sketch rehearsal
jokes.punchline: 'I think he's trying out a new Lebanese thing' — a completely unintelligible explanation for Larry's bizarre Tarzan accent, delivered with confidence
jokes.explanation: 'Lebanese thing' is wonderfully specific nonsense — it's funny because it's stated with conviction about something that makes no sense. The writers' behind-the-scenes cynicism about their own host is authentic showbiz satire, and 'Lebanese' as the chosen specificity is perfectly absurd.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: You know, make it more my style.

jokes.text: Artie to Larry: 'You know, talking to you is like talking to you.'
jokes.setup: Artie has been trying to manage Larry's anxiety and is running out of patience
jokes.punchline: A tautological non-statement — 'talking to you is like talking to you' — that is both a profound expression of exasperation and technically meaningless
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's single best line. 'Talking to you is like talking to you' is a Zen koan of exasperation — grammatically meaningless, emotionally precise, and instantly quotable. It communicates the full weight of Artie's exhaustion with Larry's circular anxieties without saying anything. The tautology IS the point: Larry is so specifically, uniquely frustrating that no comparison exists. Rip Torn's delivery would make this legendary. Comparable in craft and memorability to the show's best lines.

dialogue.speaker: Spider Expert
dialogue.line: I carry a spider anti-venom kit on my person at all times. I didn't bring it with me today.

jokes.text: Larry: 'I can't go on with this spider thing, Arty.' Artie: 'Listen, consider it canceled.' — immediate, no hesitation
jokes.setup: After all the buildup about the spider stunt being great television, Larry caves
jokes.punchline: Artie cancels it instantly — all his 'huge laughs' advocacy evaporates the moment Larry pushes back, showing his real priority is managing Larry, not the show
jokes.explanation: The comedic payoff to all of Artie's hard-selling is this instantaneous capitulation. It's funny because it reveals that Artie's conviction was always entirely contingent on Larry's mood — the 'huge laughs' were never the actual goal. A quiet but sharp joke about the real dynamics of showbiz management.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: It's not easy being on this side of the cue cards.

jokes.text: Artie identifies a Quick Light Briquets commercial featuring Hank and makes a joke: 'Let me guess. This is Quick Light Briquets, is it? The fastest light in the West. Fire 'em up, partner.'
jokes.setup: Artie sees Hank filming a commercial
jokes.punchline: Artie delivers the commercial tagline himself — 'Fire 'em up, partner' — as if he's seen it many times, or as if it's self-evidently terrible
jokes.explanation: A light scene-setter that establishes the comedy of Hank doing commercial work — slightly diminished status compared to the main host. Not a strong punchline but functional showbiz satire.

dialogue.speaker: Carol
dialogue.line: Your check is on the way.

jokes.text: Artie asks Hank to do the spider stunt 'instead of Larry' — claiming Larry himself requested it
jokes.setup: Larry has canceled the spider stunt; Artie needs an alternative
jokes.punchline: Artie volunteers Hank under false pretenses — claiming Larry 'himself wants you to handle this stunt' when we just watched Larry cancel it — Hank's credulity makes him the perfect mark
jokes.explanation: The comedy is structural — the audience knows the lie being told and can anticipate Hank's gullibility. Artie's manipulation of Hank is a recurring dynamic, and the specific false attribution ('Larry himself wants you') is a nicely cynical move.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: You actually have to get earmuffs at a specialty shop?

jokes.text: Hank: 'This isn't happening because Larry knows I'm unhappy, is it?' Artie: 'You're unhappy?'
jokes.setup: Hank is suspicious that the spider stunt offer is a consolation prize for his unhappiness
jokes.punchline: Artie's response — 'You're unhappy?' — is performed with complete genuine surprise, as if Hank's chronic discontent is news, despite it being the defining trait of everyone's relationship with him
jokes.explanation: Artie's performed ignorance of Hank's obvious unhappiness is a great character bit. The response 'You're unhappy?' — not dismissive, but genuinely inquiring — is the kind of executive maneuver that keeps Hank off-balance. It's both funny and reveals Artie's management style.

dialogue.speaker: Carol
dialogue.line: maybe you could talk to costumes about getting you a longer loincloth. I saw your balls.

jokes.text: Hank: 'Not at all. I'm always looking for opportunities to showcase my versatility. Not that I've made a stink about it, because I am not a squeaky wheel.'
jokes.setup: Artie asks if Hank is unhappy; Hank is clearly very unhappy
jokes.punchline: Hank's denial is so comprehensive and over-qualified — 'versatility,' 'not made a stink,' 'not a squeaky wheel' — that it constitutes a full confession of exactly the opposite
jokes.explanation: Peak Hank. The denial speech is perfect Tambor territory — every qualification is a tell, every denial confirms the complaint. 'Not a squeaky wheel' from someone who is demonstrably the squeakiest wheel in the building is great character irony. Jeffrey Tambor would make this sing.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: You're wrong right there. They're clearly found in plastic boxes.

jokes.text: Larry learns the sketch is canceled because Carol thinks it sucks. Larry: 'She's right. Cancel it.' — no hesitation
jokes.setup: Larry is told Carol Burnett wants to cancel their sketch
jokes.punchline: Larry's immediate agreement — 'She's right. Cancel it.' — is both self-aware and a funny reversal of his earlier eagerness
jokes.explanation: Larry's immediate capitulation to Carol's judgment — not even a token defense of the sketch — reveals both his genuine self-awareness as a performer and his deference to Burnett's legendary status. Quick and efficient.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I've never complained about anyone opening up a lid of anything.

jokes.text: Larry: 'Between you and me, I'm relieved. I looked like an idiot in that loincloth.' Artie: 'Between you and me, I think I saw your balls at one point.'
jokes.setup: Larry confesses private relief about the sketch being canceled
jokes.punchline: Artie's private confidence mirrors Larry's syntax exactly ('between you and me') but delivers a devastating visual — he saw Larry's balls — as the reciprocal confession
jokes.explanation: Beautifully constructed exchange. The structural mirroring — 'between you and me' used twice — sets up the parallel confession, and what Artie confides is so much more damaging and funny than Larry's. The loincloth visual is established, the payoff is earned, and the delivery of 'I think I saw your balls at one point' with Artie's characteristic gravity makes it funnier. One of the episode's top five moments.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Wrong. Come on, don't you folks wanna see Hank put that on his...

jokes.text: Larry: 'That's the only laugh I got, I think.'
jokes.setup: Artie has just revealed he saw Larry's genitals during rehearsal
jokes.punchline: Larry treats accidental genital exposure as a legitimate comedic strategy that 'got a laugh' — the sad acceptance that it was his best moment
jokes.explanation: A perfect topper to the 'balls' exchange. Larry's resignation — cataloguing the accidental exposure as his comedy highlight — is both self-deprecating and pathetic in the best way. The 'I think' qualifier is a nice touch of uncertainty.

dialogue.speaker: Carol
dialogue.line: If you guys are too chicken, I'll do it.

jokes.text: Larry: 'Did you really see my balls?' — beat
jokes.setup: Larry has been discussing the sketch; the ball-sighting comes up again
jokes.punchline: Larry circling back to confirm the ball-sighting with genuine concern — the repetition reveals this is actually bothering him more than the sketch being canceled
jokes.explanation: The callback is the joke — Larry can't let it go. His need to get confirmation reveals that the ball exposure is nagging at him more than his failed sketch. The unspoken follow-up scene (we don't get Artie's response) makes it funnier. Running gag starting to develop.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: And you were 'mistakener.'

jokes.text: Artie to Hank about the meeting with Larry: 'For God's sakes, come in.'
jokes.setup: Hank approaches Larry's office timidly
jokes.punchline: Artie's exasperation at Hank's hesitation — 'For God's sakes' — frames the whole subsequent scene as a delicate diplomatic operation
jokes.explanation: A small scene-entry reaction beat. Functional but thin — works as character texture rather than a real joke.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Don't you drop me!

jokes.text: Hank enters and immediately says, 'I'm sorry. If you and Darlene are talking, I can always come back.' Artie: 'I am not talking to her. Come in.' Darlene: 'Tell him why you were here.' Darlene: 'I don't remember.'
jokes.setup: Hank enters Larry's office to find Artie with Darlene
jokes.punchline: Darlene's inability or unwillingness to recall why she was there — a small comic beat of witnessed awkwardness — is funnier than anything said directly
jokes.explanation: The rhythm of the scene — Hank's social anxiety, Artie's irritation, Darlene's blithe non-explanation — creates a small cringe-comedy texture. 'I don't remember' as a complete non-account is slightly funny but the scene mainly sets up the Hank-Larry interaction.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: It wasn't a sketch. It was a massive spastic fuck-up.

jokes.text: Hank discovers the hockey cup in Larry's office: 'What is this?' Artie: 'That's my cup from the hockey segment.'
jokes.setup: Hank picks up an unusual object in Larry's office
jokes.punchline: Artie possessively identifies the hockey groin protector as 'my cup' — the ownership claim on a jockstrap left in someone's office is slightly absurd
jokes.explanation: A small callback visual gag — the cup left in the office is a background joke. Artie claiming it as his is mildly funny. Thin but functional.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: It made the Ed Ames tomahawk throw look like a big piece of shit.

jokes.text: Larry lies to Hank — tells him the real reason for being given the spider stunt is because he wants Hank 'to express your unique creativity and flair' — Hank buys it completely
jokes.setup: Larry needs to tell Hank why he's being given the spider stunt without revealing it's because Larry is afraid
jokes.punchline: Larry constructs a speech so transparently false — 'unique creativity and flair' applied to putting spiders on your arm — that it's cringe comedy; Hank's pathetic gratitude makes it worse
jokes.explanation: Classic cringe sitcom construction — the audience knows what's really happening, and watching Hank receive this transparent manipulation with deep gratitude is both funny and a little sad. Larry's cowardice and Hank's need for validation are both exposed simultaneously. The show's core dynamic in miniature.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Oh, no, the spider guy said it's a mild allergic reaction. It should run its course in about a week's time... and it's hardly noticeable.

jokes.text: Hank, deeply moved by Larry's fake speech: '...A little uncomfortable right now, but... My God... you're a good man.'
jokes.setup: Larry has delivered a completely false speech about valuing Hank's creativity
jokes.punchline: Hank is so starved for validation that a transparently fake speech makes him emotional — 'My God, you're a good man' said with genuine feeling
jokes.explanation: This is the cringe peak of the Hank arc in this episode. 'My God, you're a good man' delivered with complete sincerity in response to an obvious lie is devastating — it's funny and sad simultaneously. Jeffrey Tambor's ability to play genuine feeling in ironic contexts is the show's secret weapon, and this line is pure Hank: his neediness laid bare. The comedy comes from the gap between what we know and what Hank believes.

jokes.text: Extended physical bit: Hank tries to hug Larry — the hug goes on far too long — Larry: 'Hank, please.'
jokes.setup: Hank, emotionally overwhelmed by Larry's fake speech, moves in for a hug
jokes.punchline: The hug exceeds all normal duration; Larry's eventual 'Hank, please' at the 10-second mark is the verbal boundary; the physical comedy is in the sustained discomfort
jokes.explanation: Great sustained cringe comedy. The extended hug is the kind of protracted awkward moment that the show specialized in — the audience watching Larry try to endure Hank's emotional overflow is physically uncomfortable in the best way. 'Hank, please' as the eventual protest is perfectly understated.

jokes.text: Carol Burnett to Hank during commercial filming: 'Could you take your top off? I'm begging you. Could you?'
jokes.setup: Hank is filming a commercial with Carol Burnett
jokes.punchline: Carol asking Hank to remove his shirt — the comedy being that this is the last request you'd expect directed at Hank, and Carol's 'I'm begging you' suggests it's for the comedy, not the aesthetics
jokes.explanation: A quick gag playing on Hank's physique — Carol's 'I'm begging you' implies the comedy, not desire. Light but functional.

jokes.text: Hank's 'Hey, Now' exchange with Carol Burnett: 'Tremendous.' / 'Hey, now.' / 'Hey, now.'
jokes.setup: Hank has been given an opportunity to do the spider stunt; meeting Carol, he delivers his catchphrase
jokes.punchline: Carol Burnett — a genuine comedy legend — responds to Hank's 'Hey, now' with her own 'Hey, now,' creating a moment of false equivalence that's both affectionate and slightly absurd
jokes.explanation: The joke is Carol Burnett's willingness to play along with Hank's catchphrase, which she likely doesn't know, treating it as a genuine exchange of pleasantries. Hank's 'Tremendous' — his default word for good news — before the Hey Now is also a small character comedy beat. The moment is light but well-placed.

jokes.text: Hank casually tells Larry he's doing the spider thing 'tonight' — Larry's reaction beat
jokes.setup: Hank has been manipulated into taking the spider stunt; now he mentions it to Larry as if he volunteered
jokes.punchline: Larry's reaction — absorbing that his cowardice is now Hank's public moment — should be a visible wince or pause; the irony is that Hank is excited to do the thing Larry was too scared to do
jokes.explanation: An irony beat — the audience knows the full chain of events, so watching Hank announce his spider heroics to Larry is a quiet joke about the politics of cowardice. Works on rewatch when you can appreciate all the moving parts.

jokes.text: Hank asks the writers to 'put a different crank on' the spider material to 'make it more my style'
jokes.setup: Hank is preparing for the spider stunt he was manipulated into doing
jokes.punchline: 'A different crank on it' — Hank's specific idiom for customizing material, plus the implication that his comedic 'style' is distinct enough to require a rewrite for a stunt involving sitting still while spiders crawl on you
jokes.explanation: Hank's self-importance expressing itself in industry jargon ('put a different crank on it') while requesting customization for a stunt that requires zero performance skill is a good character beat. The writers' deadpan 'Yeah, we'll get right on that' is the deserved punchline.

jokes.text: Spider handler reveals he carries an anti-venom kit 'on my person at all times' — then: 'I didn't bring it with me today.'
jokes.setup: Hank asks if he'll get bitten; handler reassures him he carries anti-venom at all times
jokes.punchline: 'I didn't bring it with me today' — the safety net doesn't exist for this specific appointment
jokes.explanation: A perfect structure: the reassurance is built up fully before being dismantled in six words. The gap between 'I always carry it' and 'not today' is maximal, and the nonchalance of the handler makes it funnier. Clean joke construction.

jokes.text: Hank notices a burn mark on the spider handler's arm and asks about it. Handler: 'It's a burn. I burned myself on the iron.' — with a spider bite visible to the audience
jokes.setup: Handler says Hank absolutely won't get bitten; Hank notices what appears to be a bite mark
jokes.punchline: The handler insists it's just an iron burn — almost certainly a spider bite — delivered with complete confidence
jokes.explanation: A dark comedy visual gag — the handler's reassurance is immediately undercut by physical evidence on his own body. The audience can see the subtext clearly. Good escalation of the spider-danger joke.

jokes.text: Handler: 'Absolutely not [you won't get bitten]... but if you should get bitten, it'll only hurt for a second... unless you're allergic to spider bites.' Hank: 'Okay, so, how would I know if I were allergic?' Handler: 'Well, you'd go to a doctor and have yourself checked.' — 'And if I were allergic... what could happen?' — Handler: 'Oh, my.'
jokes.setup: Handler is reassuring Hank about spider safety
jokes.punchline: 'Oh, my.' — the handler's response to what happens if you're allergic and get bitten is so bad he won't even say it; the non-answer is the answer
jokes.explanation: 'Oh, my.' as the answer to 'what could happen if I'm allergic?' is a beautifully understated response to catastrophe. The escalation from 'it'll only hurt for a second' to 'oh, my' — with the handler refusing to elaborate — implies something so terrible it can't be named. The structure (progressive reassurance followed by progressive revelation of horror) is well-built. One of the episode's funnier exchanges.

jokes.text: Hank asks if he'll get bitten. Wrangler: 'Absolutely not... but if you should get bitten, it'll only hurt for a second... unless you're allergic to spider bites.'
jokes.setup: Hank asks for a guarantee he won't be bitten
jokes.punchline: The wrangler's 'Absolutely not' immediately dissolves into a cascade of qualifications — 'but if you should... unless you're allergic' — each one a deeper layer of potential catastrophe, delivered in the same flat reassuring tone
jokes.explanation: An escalating reassurance that systematically destroys itself. The structure is textbook: absolute guarantee → minor exception → major exception (allergy). Each clause that should comfort actually terrifies. The deadpan delivery — same tone throughout — is what makes this sing. Connected to joke 57, this is a sustained two-beat horror comedy riff from the wrangler.

jokes.text: Larry, off-camera in a separate scene: 'So was I wrong? Hank really wanted to do the spider thing... You know, the audience would rather see me do it, I think. Wouldn't they?'
jokes.setup: Larry is rationalizing giving the stunt to Hank
jokes.punchline: Larry reverse-engineers his cowardice into altruism (Hank 'really wanted' it) then can't help undermining Hank ('the audience would rather see me') — revealing both self-deception and competitive insecurity in adjacent sentences
jokes.explanation: Excellent Larry Sanders character comedy. He convinces himself of Hank's genuine enthusiasm while simultaneously undercutting him — both moves are self-serving and he doesn't notice the contradiction. The 'I think. Wouldn't they?' seeking validation even from an off-camera interlocutor is perfect Larry.

jokes.text: Larry: 'It's not easy being on this side of the cue cards.' — then demonstrates by holding the cue cards wrong
jokes.setup: Larry is making the point that it's hard to be a talk show host rather than a guest
jokes.punchline: He holds up cue cards to show it's hard — the visual joke being that he's using cue cards for an informal conversation, then demonstrating them incorrectly
jokes.explanation: A meta-joke about the mechanics of being a talk show host. The physical demonstration with cue cards is a light visual gag. Works better as a character beat than a straight joke.

jokes.text: Carol tells the story of her ear-pull signal to her grandmother — 'It meant, Hi, I'm fine. Your check is on the way.'
jokes.setup: Carol explains the famous ear-pull gesture was a signal to her grandmother who raised her
jokes.punchline: 'Your check is on the way' — the earful signal encodes both affection and financial obligation; the specificity makes it funnier than a simpler sentiment
jokes.explanation: A real bit of Carol Burnett lore rendered funny by the mercenary addition — 'your check is on the way.' The gesture combines 'I love you' and 'I'm paying you' into one signal, which is both touching and comic about the nature of showbiz families. Works because it has real character specificity.

jokes.text: Larry, after Carol says her earlobe is a quarter-inch longer than the other: 'Wow. You actually have to get earmuffs at a specialty shop?'
jokes.setup: A journalist measured Carol's earlobe — it's a quarter-inch longer from years of pulling
jokes.punchline: Larry's extrapolation — asymmetric earlobes requiring specialty earmuffs — is both absurd and delivered as a sincere follow-up question
jokes.explanation: A lovely on-air Larry joke. The leap from 'quarter-inch longer earlobe' to 'specialty earmuffs' is both absurd and follows its own internal logic — if one ear is bigger, how do earmuffs work? Delivered as a sincere question, which is the right call. Shows Larry's on-air persona at his best.

jokes.text: Carol: 'I'm delightful, aren't I?' — self-directed, slightly arch
jokes.setup: Carol has been sharing charming personal details about her ear
jokes.punchline: Carol announces her own delightfulness — the self-aware self-promotion is both funny and completely accurate, which makes it funnier
jokes.explanation: Three words, perfect economy. Carol's self-aware self-congratulation works because she is genuinely delightful — the joke is the audacity of saying it, and the fact that it's true makes the self-promotion charming rather than obnoxious.

jokes.text: Larry and Carol both claim they 'loved' the Tarzan sketch rehearsal and wish they could have done it — each sentence more effusive, building to 'I love doing broad, physical comedy'/'You're great at it'/'I wish we could've done it'/'Me too'/'Me too'
jokes.setup: Both Larry and Carol said privately that the sketch was terrible and they're relieved it's canceled
jokes.punchline: They now perform mutual enthusiasm for a sketch they both privately hated — the showbiz politeness ritual rendered as gentle comedy
jokes.explanation: Smart structural comedy — the audience has seen both parties separately admit the sketch was terrible, so watching them perform mutual enthusiasm is cringe irony. The escalating 'me too / me too' is a particularly good touch — showbiz social rituals captured perfectly.

jokes.text: Carol: 'I saw your balls.' Larry: 'What?' Carol: 'I saw your balls.'
jokes.setup: Carol has just recommended a longer loincloth
jokes.punchline: Carol, with complete composure, states the revelation directly — twice — while Larry's 'What?' implies he hoped it was a loincloth-design suggestion and not a confession
jokes.explanation: The episode's comic peak. The running ball-exposure joke reaches its apex when Carol Burnett — a television legend — delivers the line with complete matter-of-fact composure. The repetition ('I saw your balls... I saw your balls.') after Larry's incredulous 'What?' is perfect: she's not embarrassed or gleeful, just stating fact. The comedy of Carol Burnett, of all people, saying this to Larry Sanders cannot be overstated. Maximum economy, maximum impact, perfect payoff to a carefully built multi-scene callback.

jokes.text: Post-commercial break: Hank clearly allergic/distressed from spider — Larry notices during show and asks 'Hank, are you all right? A little mop up.'
jokes.setup: Hank has done the spider stunt; he's now visibly reacting
jokes.punchline: 'A little mop up' — Larry's on-air understatement for what is apparently a significant allergic reaction, maintaining professionalism while Hank suffers
jokes.explanation: A good deadpan reaction beat — 'a little mop up' as professional euphemism for an on-air medical emergency is the kind of show-must-go-on comedy the series does well.

jokes.text: Hank anxious before air: 'Listen, this Steve, this spider guy... is he on the up and up?' Artie: 'Don't worry about it, Hank. The spiders are real. ...He had some concern about an allergic reaction.'
jokes.setup: Hank is asking Artie for last-minute reassurance right before going on air with the spiders
jokes.punchline: Artie's reassurance ('The spiders are real') immediately segues into mentioning the allergic reaction concern — one thing Hank did not need to hear with five seconds to air
jokes.explanation: Artie at his most inadvertently devastating — mentioning the allergic reaction concern as a footnote to reassurance, moments before Hank goes on air. The timing (countdown begins immediately after) is a great structural joke about the cruelty of information arriving too late to help.

jokes.text: On-air: Larry, gesturing at plastic spider boxes: 'Well, Steve, I see you brought your lunch with you.'
jokes.setup: Steve Kutcher arrives on set carrying boxes of spiders
jokes.punchline: Larry's quip that the boxes of spiders look like a packed lunch — an on-air host joke in the Letterman/Carson tradition
jokes.explanation: A classic late-night filler joke — not original but competently delivered. The kind of throwaway that hosts use to fill while a guest settles in. Functional, not memorable.

jokes.text: Steve says the spiders are 'found in the tropical regions, desert regions of the world.' Larry: 'You're wrong right there. They're clearly found in plastic boxes.'
jokes.setup: Steve is giving factual information about tarantula habitats
jokes.punchline: Larry pedantically corrects him by reference to the specific plastic boxes in front of them — technically correct in the most literal possible way
jokes.explanation: A nicely constructed bit of absurdist pedantry. Larry's 'correction' is technically accurate while being completely unhelpful, and his confidence ('You're wrong right there') is the perfect delivery. Good late-night host joke that feels grounded in Larry's character — he's trying to be funny while also genuinely uncomfortable.

jokes.text: Larry: 'I've never complained about anyone opening up a lid of anything.'
jokes.setup: Steve asks permission to open the spider box
jokes.punchline: Larry's philosophical non-objection to lid-opening as a principle — a weirdly specific statement of policy delivered with mock gravity
jokes.explanation: A light deadpan bit. The over-formal articulation of a non-policy about lid-opening is a good Larry on-air voice moment — using formality to mask anxiety.

jokes.text: Steve: 'I can demonstrate how you can control them crawling up a person's arm... Like you.' Larry: 'Wrong. You mean like Hank.'
jokes.setup: Steve is about to demonstrate the spider-crawling on Larry
jokes.punchline: Larry's instant deflection to Hank — 'Wrong' — delivered on-air with no preamble is both funny and a public abdication
jokes.explanation: Larry's public-facing cowardice at its funniest. 'Wrong.' — one word, delivered on national television — is the kind of bold host deflection that exposes the machinery behind the show. The audience doesn't know the behind-the-scenes context, which makes it play as host hijinks; we know, which makes it play as craven cowardice. Both are funny. The economy is excellent.

jokes.text: Larry tries to stir audience support: 'Come on, don't you folks wanna see Hank put that on his...' — reaction beat — then audience: 'Now tell the truth... wouldn't you rather see Larry?' Crowd: 'Yeah!'
jokes.setup: Larry is trying to direct the spider onto Hank; Carol and the audience redirect it back to Larry
jokes.punchline: The audience turns on Larry — 'wouldn't you rather see Larry?' eliciting a 'Yeah!' — a public democratic rejection of Larry's cowardice on his own show
jokes.explanation: Good structural comedy — the entire spider arc culminates in the audience overriding the host on his own show. Larry's attempt to route the spiders to Hank is defeated by public vote, which is both a satisfying narrative beat and a good joke about the fragility of host authority.

jokes.text: Carol: 'If you guys are too chicken, I'll do it.' — and then does, unflinchingly
jokes.setup: Larry and Hank are both visibly reluctant; the spider stunt is stalling
jokes.punchline: Carol Burnett — a 60-year-old comedy legend — steps up and does it without hesitation, shaming both men
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in the contrast — the woman who doesn't need the stunt is the only one willing to do it. Carol's unflinching participation shames both Larry and Hank and inverts the episode's entire setup. Her character is the punchline to the episode's A-plot.

jokes.text: After Larry finally takes the spider: 'And Carol, you thought I was...' Carol: 'I thought you were yeller.' Larry: 'And you were mistakener.'
jokes.setup: Larry has finally agreed to take the spider on his arm
jokes.punchline: 'Mistakener' — not a real word, a constructed comparative of 'mistaken' following 'yeller' (from Old Yeller) — Larry making up grammar to complete the parallel
jokes.explanation: 'Mistakener' is a great invented word — the logical extension of Carol's 'yeller' that doesn't actually exist but works grammatically by analogy. It's the kind of spontaneous-seeming constructed language gag that Shandling excels at. Feels like an improv beat that was kept.

jokes.text: Larry, with spider on his arm: 'Which movies was he in? All right. Now, okay...' — attempts to look away — 'I am going to look this way.'
jokes.setup: Spider is being placed on Larry's arm during live broadcast
jokes.punchline: Larry's attempt to engage professionally ('which movies was he in?') while clearly about to have a breakdown — 'I am going to look this way' is the coping mechanism announcement
jokes.explanation: Good cringe comedy — Larry trying to maintain professional interviewer mode while a spider walks on him, the gradual crumble expressed in small declarations. 'I am going to look this way' as a self-directed instruction is a nice touch.

jokes.text: Larry: 'This is not so bad. I can barely feel...' — long pause — 'Oh, my God! Carol, there's one on your shoulder.'
jokes.setup: Larry has been gradually calming down with the spider on his arm
jokes.punchline: Just as Larry achieves equanimity, a second spider is discovered on Carol — his composure shatters instantly
jokes.explanation: Classic escalation structure — the moment of triumph ('this is not so bad') immediately inverted by a new complication. The 'Oh, my God!' arrival destroys the composure he just achieved. Solid physical comedy escalation.

jokes.text: 'Don't you drop me!' — a spider (presumably) speaking or Larry in spider-panic during chaos
jokes.setup: The spider segment has descended into chaos — spiders loose, Carol panicking, Larry panicking
jokes.punchline: 'Don't you drop me!' shouted during the melee — either to someone or to a spider, which would make no sense, which makes it funnier
jokes.explanation: A panic shout during the physical chaos sequence. Funnier in context — the ambiguity of who's being addressed (a person? a spider?) adds to the mayhem. Works as part of the escalating stunt disaster.

jokes.text: After the chaos: Artie to Larry: 'Come on, it was great, Larry.' Larry: 'We killed $75,000 worth of spiders, Arty.' Artie: 'We got $100,000 worth of laughs.'
jokes.setup: The spider segment has ended in catastrophe — spiders apparently destroyed
jokes.punchline: Artie's show-business accounting: $75K of spiders = $100K of laughs. The producer's ROI calculation on arachnid deaths is both darkly funny and perfectly Artie
jokes.explanation: A great Artie line. The transactional framing of dead spiders as a cost-benefit ledger ('$75K worth of spiders... $100K worth of laughs') is both darkly funny and character-perfect — Artie treats everything, including death, as production economics. The confidence and the specific dollar amounts make it sing. Rip Torn delivers this kind of line better than anyone.

jokes.text: Artie: 'It wasn't a sketch. It was a massive spastic fuck-up.' Larry: 'Tomato, tomato. It was broad physical comedy. It made the Ed Ames tomahawk throw look like a big piece of shit.'
jokes.setup: Larry describes the spider chaos as a 'massive spastic fuck-up'; Artie spins it
jokes.punchline: 'Tomato, tomato' — as if the two descriptions are equivalent — then the Ed Ames tomahawk throw reference: comparing their spider chaos favorably to one of the most famous accidental comedy moments in TV history
jokes.explanation: The Ed Ames tomahawk throw reference is a sharp insider callback — it's one of the most famous accidental comedy moments in talk show history (a tomahawk landing in a mannequin's crotch on The Tonight Show). Artie citing it as a benchmark ('look like a big piece of shit' compared to their disaster) is both funny in isolation and a rich showbiz-insider reference. 'Tomato, tomato' as an equivalence between 'fuck-up' and 'comedy' is also a great, fast punchline.

jokes.text: Larry: 'Yeah. Really?' — genuinely pleased by the Ed Ames comparison, pausing to absorb it
jokes.setup: Artie has compared their spider disaster favorably to the Ed Ames tomahawk throw
jokes.punchline: Larry's 'Yeah. Really?' — a beat of genuine ego-gratification — he's so pleased by the comparison that he needs a moment; the pause before 'Well, I did overcome my fear, didn't I?' shows the self-story reassembling
jokes.explanation: A perfect Larry beat — his insecurity and his ego trading places in a two-word exchange. 'Yeah. Really?' is simultaneously 'is that true?' and 'of course that's true, tell me more.' Character comedy in miniature.

jokes.text: Artie: 'It made the Ed Ames tomahawk throw look like a big piece of shit.'
jokes.setup: Artie is praising the spider chaos as great television
jokes.punchline: He invokes the legendary 1965 Ed Ames tomahawk incident on The Tonight Show as the benchmark for accidental TV comedy — and claims the spider segment surpassed it, which is high (absurd) praise
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's very best lines. The Ed Ames tomahawk throw is a genuine piece of TV history — the legendary accidentally-phallic tomahawk throw on The Tonight Show — and invoking it as the comparison point for the spider chaos is an inspired industry insider reference. The fact that Artie says the spider segment made it 'look like a big piece of shit' (i.e., surpassed it) is the darkly hilarious verdict of a veteran producer. 'Made the Ed Ames tomahawk throw look like a big piece of shit' is a phrase that will delight anyone who knows the reference and be explained for generations. Character integration is near-perfect: only someone of Artie's era and experience would reach for this comparison. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Larry: 'Well, I did overcome my fear, didn't I?' Artie: 'Yes, for a second... until you flung that poor creature to a fiery death.'
jokes.setup: Larry is self-congratulating on overcoming his spider fear
jokes.punchline: 'For a second... until you flung that poor creature to a fiery death' — Artie's qualification is so devastating and specific ('fiery death') that it erases Larry's accomplishment entirely
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode. The structure is perfect — Larry builds himself up, Artie partially confirms, then the qualifier annihilates everything with forensic precision. 'Until you flung that poor creature to a fiery death' is not just funny; it reveals what actually happened during the stunt (Larry panicked and killed a spider violently) and judges it with the gravity of a manslaughter verdict. 'Fiery death' is the operative phrase — specific, dark, and devastating. Artie's 'poor creature' sympathy for the spider is also a great character touch.

jokes.text: Larry: 'But in a funny way.' Artie: 'For a hundred times, yes.'
jokes.setup: Larry is trying to salvage his reputation after the 'fiery death' revelation
jokes.punchline: 'For a hundred times, yes' — Artie's weary, exaggerated affirmation; not just 'yes' but an exhausted 'yes a hundred times over,' suggesting he's been doing this for Larry for decades
jokes.explanation: 'For a hundred times, yes' is a great Artie line — it's not sarcasm, it's exhausted sincerity. He has been telling Larry his disasters are funny for their entire professional relationship. The 'hundred times' scale implies a history of exactly this kind of scene. Character-specific and perfectly economical.

jokes.text: Hank's post-spider reassurance: 'The spider guy said it's a mild allergic reaction. It should run its course in about a week's time, and it's hardly noticeable.'
jokes.setup: Hank has been bitten by a spider (the allergy the wrangler worried about earlier has manifested)
jokes.punchline: 'Hardly noticeable' — said about what is presumably a visible and unpleasant allergic reaction, combined with the wrangler's 'Oh, my' foreshadowing — is a perfect callback payoff and ironic understatement. The week-long duration adds insult.
jokes.explanation: A satisfying triple callback: pays off (1) the wrangler's ominous 'Oh, my' about allergy consequences, (2) the wife's wish that a spider would bite him, and (3) Hank's general trajectory of being volunteered for what Larry refused. 'Hardly noticeable' as a euphemism for whatever is happening to Hank's face/body is a great ironic understatement. The week-long duration adds dark comedy — this won't be over quickly.

jokes.text: Post-show: 'Oh, no, the spider guy said it's a mild allergic reaction. It should run its course in about a week's time... and it's hardly noticeable.' — then someone clearly sees it's very noticeable — beat — 'Yeah? Nothing.'
jokes.setup: Hank has apparently had an allergic reaction to the spider; someone is checking on him
jokes.punchline: 'Yeah? Nothing.' — the person looking at Hank's visible allergic reaction says nothing, which implies it's bad enough to silence them
jokes.explanation: The callback to the allergic reaction concern pays off beautifully — and the payoff is a silence. 'Nothing' after 'Yeah?' is the visual joke (we see or infer a grotesque allergic response), and the silence is more damning than any description. Excellent callback resolution, economical and dark.

jokes.text: Artie signs off: 'Huge laughs, Hank. Huge laughs, Larry. Huge.'
jokes.setup: The episode ends with the aftermath of the spider stunt
jokes.punchline: Artie returns to his signature 'huge laughs' phrase from the beginning of the episode — now tinged with irony given everything that happened — but delivered with the same conviction
jokes.explanation: The episode's closing callback is earned and resonant. 'Huge laughs, Hank. Huge laughs, Larry. Huge.' returns to Artie's original hard-sell phrase, now colored by everything that has happened — spiders killed, Hank allergic, sketches abandoned. But Artie delivers it with the same conviction. This is the show's thesis: in show business, the spin never stops. The three-part structure (Hank, Larry, Huge) is perfect escalating economy. One of the episode's best moments structurally.

tmdb_overview: Larry battles his reluctance when real live spiders are scheduled for the show, and tries to find a sketch to do with guest Carol Burnett.
